newsitem.title: USA: Officials reject Gulf War illness coverup charge.
newsitem.headline: Officials reject Gulf War illness coverup charge.

text.p: The CIA and the Pentagon dismissed as unfair and illogical on Wednesday a charge by two former CIA analysts that the government was hiding evidence of scores of incidents in which Americans may have been exposed to Iraqi chemical weapons during the 1991 Gulf War.

The husband-and-wife intelligence analysts, Patrick and Robin Eddington, told the New York Times they had turned up evidence of as many as 60 incidents in which nerve gas and other chemical weapons were released near U.S. troops.

They said the CIA and the Pentagon sought to hinder their unauthorised investigation, carried out before they resigned from the agency this year, and to bury the truth. They said their probe raised concern at the highest levels of the CIA and the Defence Department including from John Deutch, then the Pentagon official responsible for investigating Gulf War illnesses and now the director of central intelligence.

Patrick Eddington, who is 33 and planning to write a book outlining his case against the Central Intelligence Agency, told the New York Times government officials who had overseen investigations of Gulf War illnesses "are continuing to lie, are continuing to withhold information."
Denying these charges, the CIA said the Eddingtons, trained to read satellite imagery, were trying to portray an honest difference among intelligence analysts as a coverup.

"To label a difference of opinion a coverup is just unfair, illogical and plain wrong," said David Christian, a CIA spokesman. He said when higher-level CIA officials learned of the Eddingtons' unauthorised probe their thesis was given a complete hearing by the agency's "all-source" analysts -- those who review raw intelligence from the full range of human and technical sources, as distinct from photoanalysis alone.
"Their findings just did not pass a peer review," he said. He said the CIA this year turned over the raw intelligence at issue to a White House panel investigating Gulf War illnesses.

Shortly after serving in the war, some military men and women reported unexplained problems such as fatigue, muscle and joint pain, memory loss and severe headaches that have become known collectively as Gulf War illness. But there has been no proven link to exposure to Iraqi chemicals and the government says it had no evidence until recently that large numbers of Americans may have been exposed to Iraqi chemicals.
"The idea that the Defence Department has engaged in any conspiracy to cover up any information regarding Persian Gulf illnesses is simply not true," spokesman Bryan Whitman said.
